title: Architecture & Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance, and ADRs
author: Ava Martinez
summary: Canonical, cross-cutting architecture and engineering standards for Redwood Inference covering API design, code conventions, infra requirements, model-serving best practices, observability conventions, performance SLOs, and a set of canonical ADRs for recent architectural decisions.
body:
Overview

Purpose
- Provide a single reference for teams building services and features on Redwood Inference.
- Reduce design churn by standardizing API patterns, code practices, infra requirements, observability signals, and performance goals.
- Surface the authoritative ADRs that constrain implementation choices.

Scope
This document applies to all services and components that support public or internal APIs, model-serving endpoints, and orchestration layers across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private products. It is intended for engineers, product owners, and SREs.

1) API Standards
- Use RESTful resource-oriented APIs for management/control plane endpoints; use gRPC or HTTP/2 for high-throughput internal data plane where low latency is required.
- Versioning: include a stable major version in the path (e.g., /v1/models/{id}/infer). Breaking changes require bumping the major version and an ADR.
- Idempotency: write operations that may be retried must accept an Idempotency-Key header and return 409 on true conflicts.
- Request/Response contracts:
  - Prefer JSON for control-plane responses; responses must include an envelope with metadata: {"request_id", "timestamp", "trace_id"}.
  - Streaming generation endpoints must implement chunked transfer (Transfer-Encoding: chunked) and provide event framing per the Streaming API spec in /eng-developer-experience/api-examples.
- Error handling:
  - Use standard HTTP status codes. Errors must return a JSON body with keys: code, message, retryable (true/false), details (optional).
  - Map transient infra errors to 503 with Retry-After where appropriate.
- Security:
  - All external APIs must require authentication (API key or mTLS for Private deployments).
  - Sensitive parameters must not be logged (see Data Handling section).

Example (control-plane create model):

POST /v1/models
Content-Type: application/json
Idempotency-Key: abc-123

Request body:
{
  "name": "redwood-bert-1",
  "artifact_uri": "s3://models/redwood-bert-1/",
  "deployment_profile": "gpu-standard"
}

Response (201):
{
  "request_id": "req_01F4X2",
  "model_id": "mdl_9a7f",
  "status": "creating"
}

2) Coding Standards
- Language & repo level: follow per-repo CONTRIBUTING.md conventions. Primary languages: Go for control plane, Rust/C++ for hot-path runtime, Python for tooling/evals.
- Formatting & linting:
  - Enforce gofmt/golangci-lint in CI, rustfmt and clippy for Rust, and Black/ruff for Python. CI must block merges on lint failures.
- Tests:
  - Unit tests: 80% coverage target for platform libraries; critical runtime kernels require 90%+ per ADR.
  - Integration tests: every service must include a minimal contract test that can run in CI (mocked dependencies ok).
- API contracts: use OpenAPI for REST endpoints and maintain the spec in the repo root under /openapi. Changes to the spec must include an API changelog entry.
- Code review:
  - Two approvers required for changes to platform libraries or infra IaC. One approver allowed for non-core service docs. Security-sensitive changes (auth, crypto) must include a security reviewer.

3) Infrastructure Standards
- IaC and provisioning:
  - All long-lived infra must be declared in Terraform. Short-lived test infra may use tooling but must include a terraform drift procedure.
  - State management: Terraform remote state in an encrypted S3 bucket with state locking via DynamoDB.
- Networking:
  - Default VPC design: segmented subnets (control-plane, data-plane, management). All cross-subnet traffic must go through audited security groups and NACLs.
- Secrets & keys:
  - Use KMS/HSM-backed key management. Secrets in CI must be stored in the approved secrets manager (Vault or cloud native).
- Capacity & sizing:
  - GPU pools: categorize as gpu-standard (A100-equivalent), gpu-high-memory (H100-equivalent), and cpu-only. Autoscaling policy templates are provided in /eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity.

4) Model-Serving Standards
- Model packaging:
  - Models must include a manifest.json with fields: name, version, inputs, tokenizer, kv_cache_supported (true/false), quantization_profile. (See model-onboarding templates.)
- Serving modes:
  - Live inference endpoints must support predictable latency SLOs (see Performance Standards). Support both streaming and non-streaming outputs.
- KV cache and state:
  - Runtime must expose KV cache metrics (hits, misses, evictions). Any service that mutates cached KV state must be tolerant of eviction and rehydration.
- Quantization & variants:
  - For every production model, maintain at least two compatible variants: high-precision (FP16/FP32) and quantized (int8 or bfloat16). Fallthrough routing policies must be declared with each model.
- Model rollout:
  - Follow rollout policy: internal canary (5% traffic for 24 hours) -> gradual increase (25% for 48 hours) -> full rollout. Rollback must be automated via traffic control and documented in the model's release notes.

5) Observability Standards
- Tracing & correlation:
  - All services must propagate trace_id and span_id. Use OpenTelemetry for instrumentation.
- Metrics:
  - Counters, gauges, and histograms must be emitted to the central metrics backend. Standard metrics: request_rate (rps), request_latency_ms (p50/p95/p99), error_rate, model_infer_tokens_per_second, kv_cache_hit_rate.
- Log conventions:
  - Structured JSON logs with keys: timestamp, level, service, env, request_id, trace_id, message. Use log levels: DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR.
- Alerts & runbooks:
  - Define alerts for SLO breaches (see Performance). Every alert must link to a runbook in /eng-platform/runbooks.

6) Performance Standards and SLOs
- Platform-level SLOs (applies to Hosted + Dedicated control plane):
  - Control-plane API availability: 99.95% monthly. Error budget: 0.05% of requests.
  - Provisioning latency (model deployment to ready): P99 < 10 minutes for pre-warmed flows, P99 < 30 minutes for cold flows.
- Data-plane (model inference) SLOs (per model profile):
  - Latency SLOs are set per deployment profile. Example profiles:
    - interactive-low-latency: p95 < 200ms, p99 < 500ms (small models, cpu/gpu-optimized kernels)
    - batching-high-throughput: average tokens/sec > 5000 for gpu-standard pools
  - KV cache hit rate target: >= 85% for workloads that enable prefix caching.
- Load testing:
  - All model-serving changes must include a perf test run against the benchmarking suite in /eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite. Include baseline numbers in PR description.

7) ADRs (Decision Records)
- Format: each ADR must contain: id, status (proposed|accepted|deferred|superseded), context, decision, consequences, and owners. Store ADRs in the repository under /docs/adrs and in Confluence under architecture-and-standards.

Canonical ADR summaries included here:

ADR-2025-09: Runtime language choice\- Status: accepted\- Context: need for deterministic, low-latency kernels and safe memory management.\- Decision: core hot-path runtime implemented in Rust with FFI bindings for CUDA kernels; control plane remains Go.\- Consequences: improved safety and performance; increases Rust hiring/skill requirements.

ADR-2026-01: Model artifact storage\- Status: accepted\- Decision: Use object storage (S3-compatible) for model artifacts with signed, time-limited URIs for runtime pulls.

ADR-2026-03: Quantization default\- Status: accepted\- Decision: Default production variant uses quantized int8 where accuracy regressions are below 1% compared to FP16 baseline. Quantization profiles must be tested against core eval prompt sets.

8) Operational Playbooks and Runbooks
- Incident playbook highlights:
  - On high error-rate alert for the inference data-plane:
    1. Verify metric (p95 latency, error rate) and correlate with recent deploys.
    2. Roll traffic to fallback model variant or region.
    3. If fallback fails, scale up gpu pool by +30% for 15 minutes and monitor.
    4. Open an incident with the oncall pager and create a postmortem template.
- Runbook links: document runbooks and pager rotation in /oncall-and-incident-response/runbooks.

9) Governance and Change Process
- Standards owner: Architecture WG (rotating chairs) owns this document. Major changes require review by Architecture WG and sign-off by Eng Director.
- Compliance: changes that affect security, privacy, or cost must include an impact assessment and a reviewer from Security or Finance as appropriate.

Appendix A: Example Terraform baseline table
| Resource | Minimum configuration | Owner | Notes |
|---|---:|---|---|
| VPC | 3 subnets (public, private, management) | infra-team | Subnet CIDR allocations documented in /eng-infra/cloud-accounts-and-networking |
| GPU pool | gpu-standard: min 2 nodes, max 50 nodes | infra-ml | Autoscaling policies in /eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity |

Appendix B: Quick CLI examples
- Validate OpenAPI spec:
  - openapi-cli validate ./openapi/spec.yaml
- Run a local perf test (example):
  - ./perf/run_benchmark --model mdl_9a7f --profile interactive-low-latency --duration 5m

Appendix C: Ownership matrix
- Architecture WG: standards owner, ADR steward
- eng-infra: Terraform, networking, capacity templates
- eng-serving-runtime: runtime kernels, KV cache, perf harness
- eng-platform: observability, tracing, alerts

How to propose a change
1. Open a PR against this document (docs/architecture/standards.md) with the proposed change.
2. Add reviewers: at least one Architecture WG member and the relevant owner (infra, runtime, platform).
3. Run the perf/compat tests referenced in the PR checklist.
4. Merge after approvals and update the ADRs if the change involves a decision.
